Open Propagate model / fit… from the representative scan. Review targets on the
source channel/stage, which is a different selection from browser overlays. Choose
independent reference/previous-success fits, simultaneous shared fitting, or model
copying. Copying does not create a fitted result.

Add 

reference-relative series bounds and overall trends
only when justified. Use explicit scan order or increasing numeric coordinates;
review a named maximum/minimum and its membership. Global sharing, soft penalties
and strict constraints express different assumptions.

If using 

two passes, stage/review pass one first, then
choose parameter-specific seeds, averaging scans, narrower bounds and sharing for
pass two. A mean seed is not an averaged spectrum or an uncertainty estimate.
Review the intended pass and Apply successful results. Staging alone leaves the
working scans unchanged; failed targets retain their work.

propagation, sharing, named-scan trends and mean-based pass-two seeds without
assigning experimental meaning to any component. Start with an unconstrained
simultaneous fit, then explore explicit trends and a second pass below.

records.content:
For an optional constrained variant, open Trends / pass-two setup… → Overall
trends, add P2_A and choose Maximum at selected scan, series-02, hard
strength and Extremum only. Choose application to both passes for this exercise.
This changes first-pass rules, so stage pass one again.

To inspect coordinate-based limits, choose numeric coordinates in the collection
dialog and enter 0, 10, 20 in that explicit order. Those are arbitrary example
units; they are not measured times or doses. An extremum-only rule does not use
their spacing. Optional maximum-slope rules do: 0.1 area/unit across these intervals
allows area differences of 1.0, whereas a different coordinate unit changes that limit.
Changing coordinates/order invalidates staged passes; stage pass one again before
configuring pass two.

For longer series choose Monotonic sides only when all intervening values should
rise/fall on their respective sides. Strict inequalities permit ties; a soft
maximum encourages rather than guarantees the relationship.

records.content:
Use Subtract current edges, a checkbox below the plot beside Focus Mode, to
see where peaks sit above the model continuum.

Add an ionisation edge if needed and give it sensible position/width/height/slope
values. It can be a working estimate; no successful fit is required.

Check Subtract current edges.

Inspect the data and total above the current edges; adjust components as needed.
Updating edge parameters updates the display immediately.

Uncheck it to restore the ordinary data/envelope view.

The display subtracts the sum of every current model edge, including additional
edges and terms whose display checkbox is hidden. The same edge sum is subtracted
from data and Total, and the edge curves themselves are hidden in this view.
Peak and linear-background curves are unchanged by edge subtraction. It does not
subtract the linear background or the other peaks. With no edges, or a zero edge
contribution, there may be no visible change.

Edge drag controls are hidden along with edge curves. Turn subtraction off to use
the 

edge handles.

The residual and optimiser continue using the original active working spectrum
and complete model. Raw arrays and prepared arrays are unchanged. This is a
display of current model subtraction, not a new prepared detector channel or
a permanently edge-corrected dataset. Fitted-curve CSVs retain their numerical
data/envelope/edge columns independently of this toggle.

For overlays, each scan uses the edges from its own displayed channel’s working
model. Overlaying scans does not apply the active model’s edge to every scan.
To make an edge follow a peak, use 

edge-to-peak linking.
For operations that change the actual working signal, see 

scan preparation.

Component display, edge subtraction and offsets

records.content:
Check Offset components on the same display row, then adjust its numeric factor.
This shifts the individual peak, edge and background curves downward, together
with their peak handles. A dotted Component zero (offset) line marks their
shifted zero; a curve below ordinary zero does not imply that its fitted area
became negative.

The shift is\Delta I = f\,\max\!\left(\max(y)-\min(y),\;\max|y|\right),

where f is the factor (initially 0.1) and y is the active working signal.
Previously saved explicit factors are restored. For a signal ranging from −0.2
to 1.8, the scale is 2.0; factor 0.1 shifts components down by 0.2 intensity unit.
Increasing the factor moves them farther
down. Factor zero gives no shift, and unchecking the toggle restores normal positions.
When no data are loaded, the model preview supplies the scale.
For an all-zero signal, the renderer uses a scale of 1.

Data, comparison scans, Total and residual do not move. Parameters and numerical
fits/exports are unchanged. The vertical view expands to include the shifted
curves while horizontal framing is retained. Drag the shifted handles normally:
the GUI removes the visual shift before converting their height back into A.
The 

drag-control screenshot
shows this arrangement.

You can combine offset components with edge subtraction. The total/data then
show the edge-subtracted view while individual component curves are displaced
below them. Focus Mode can still fade unselected components in either view.

records.content:
Drag the orange target horizontally to translate the peak, vertically to alter
its contribution, or diagonally to do both. It belongs to the individual component,
not the total envelope or data-plus-edge height. A is integrated area, so the
GUI converts the target height using the actual profile, gain and optional component
scale. It does not simply write the height into the A cell.

Use the blue line to change μ alone. For Gaussian, Lorentzian and Voigt peaks,
the maximum is at the displayed μ. For an EMG, the orange maximum is generally
to the right of its blue μ line. Moving the orange target preserves that shape
offset; it does not redefine EMG μ to be the maximum.

records.content:
While dragging the blue μ line or the position direction of the orange target,
the original Min/Max limits do not clamp the movement. They translate with μ,
preserving their original, possibly asymmetric distances. Bound lines temporarily
hide during the gesture and return on release if Show μ bounds is enabled.
For example, μ = 285.00 with Min = 284.80 and Max = 285.50 becomes μ = 288.00,
Min = 287.80 and Max = 288.50 after dragging. Infinite endpoints stay infinite.

Fixed positions remain fixed. Linked positions still follow their source/separation;
dragging a source peak moves its linked peaks and linked edges without changing
those relationships. This shortcut does not disable links or change the fit domain.
The translated interval is the hard interval used by the next fit. Table value
edits retain existing bounds; dragging a μ-bound line edits the interval without
moving μ. A completed position drag, including its new limits, is one Undo step.

A double-left-click inside the main data axes adds a new peak at that energy,
using the shape selected in Component controls. Its height is estimated from
the data above the current continuum; existing peaks stay in place. Use the
orange target or blue line to move an existing peak. The Add multiple peaks
dialog uses its own double-clicks to stage candidates for later addition; see


batch creation.

hierarchy.lvl2: Change width without changing maximum height

records.content:
Grab either green arrow endpoint. Moving it farther from the centre broadens
the component; moving it inward narrows it. Both sides update symmetrically.

Gaussian and EMG: the parameter is sigma.

Voigt: the parameter is its Gaussian sigma; gamma stays a separate table setting.

Lorentzian: the parameter is its static gamma, which can be edited graphically
but is not an optimiser variable and has no Free checkbox.

The label reports one sigma or gamma on each side, matching its numerical
parameter. The full arrow span is twice that radius. These handles do not claim
to measure the total FWHM of every lineshape.

The drag adjusts A to keep the component’s maximum height constant. A broader
peak therefore usually acquires more integrated area. Editing sigma/gamma directly
in the table instead changes only that value and can change height at constant A.
Width dragging requires a free, independent A and, for sigma, a free independent
width. If the required A falls outside its bounds, the height-preserving change
is rejected; inspect Messages rather than assuming the width control is broken.

records.content:
The purple horizontal tail arrow appears only for EMG peaks. Its origin is
the displayed μ and its length is tau. Drag its right endpoint outward for
a longer high-energy tail, or inward for a shorter tail; tau = 0 is the Gaussian
limit used by the engine. The origin is not a second free drag endpoint.

μ and sigma stay unchanged while A adjusts to preserve maximum height. The maximum
can shift horizontally as the asymmetry changes, so the orange target can move
even though the blue μ line stays still. Tau must be free/independent, A must be
free/independent, and both sets of bounds apply. This arrow is a parameter control,
not a measured width or a peak-to-peak separation.

side; it is not an EMG tail or a peak-position bound.

the purple diamond. Other fixed/linked parameters likewise retain their state:
a peak-linked E_edge cannot move independently, but its free step, width or slope
can still be edited. Edge parameter bounds continue to clamp edge drags; the
travelling-interval behaviour above applies to peak μ only. With zero gain the
height/slope response cannot be inverted, so those controls are unavailable.

records.content:
Fit a spectrum, or Apply successful results from the series workflow.

Open the Export menu and choose Fitted curves CSV… or Fit parameters CSV….

The active scan is initially checked if it has a successful fit. Check any
other desired rows, or choose Select successful fits. Uncheck rows to omit
them. Scans without a saved fit are unavailable.

Check the Detector / stage column. Each scan exports its own currently
selected detector channel. To export another channel, select it in that
scan’s Detector dropdown before opening export. Cached fits for other channels
are retained but are not silently included.

Click Export CSV…, choose a filename and save. Each menu command writes its
own CSV; choose both export commands if you need both tables.



Figure 1:Choose which retained fits to include. Exporting leaves working scans and models intact.

The export uses the last successful fitted model, separately from subsequent
parameter edits. Last fit results shows the corresponding statistics. A failed
refit retains that earlier successful result. Changing preparation invalidates
affected results; refit those channels before exporting. An older fit record
without a saved model snapshot needs a new fit before it can be exported.
Opening a different model onto the data clears the active fit statistics; fit that
model again before exporting it. Undoing model import restores the model, not a
claim that the imported model was already fitted.

CSV files use UTF-8 with a byte-order mark for Windows spreadsheet applications.
Comments containing commas, Unicode or newlines are quoted. A cancelled or failed
write preserves an existing output file. Complete editable work remains in
Save session; CSV files are numerical reports rather than restorable sessions.

Reference-calibration traces and their inspection records are preparation data,
retained in complete sessions after a successful Preview is applied. The fitted-
curve and parameter CSV commands report the selected spectra’s successful model
fits; they do not export a reference-calibration report.

Each row contains one measured energy point. Selected scans are appended in scan
table order, with identifiers repeated so the rows can be separated later.

Columns

Meaning

scan_id, scan_label, comment, source_file

Scan-table row number and source identity

detector, channel_stage

The selected signal and its retained preparation stage

energy_eV, data

Full loaded/prepared fitting arrays

fit_total

Envelope from the saved fit, including all corrections/components

residual

data - fit_total

in_fit_range

true for points within the saved fit’s domain, otherwise false

baseline, edge_total

Full-grid linear background and summed ionisation edges

peak:<name>

Individual peak contribution, including gain and component scaling

edge:<name>

Each edge contribution; the first edge is edge:primary

group:<name>

Sum of peak contributions in the named group

The full grid is exported even for a restricted fit. This preserves the engine’s
background reference; use in_fit_range to select the points actually fitted.
Zoom, Focus Mode, component visibility, visual component offsets and Subtract
current edges do not alter exported arrays. energy_eV is the data energy axis;
any fitted dE remains part of the evaluated model.

If selected scans have different components, the CSV contains the union of their
component columns. A blank component cell means that component is absent in that
scan’s model. Group sums overlap with individual peak columns; do not add group
sums to the peaks a second time when reconstructing the envelope.

This is a long table with one parameter per row, carrying the same scan/channel
identifiers. It includes component name, lineshape and peak group, fitted value,
standard error, bounds, varying/fixed/linked state, generated relationship text,
bound indication and sharing scope. Generated expressions are reported as text;
loading a CSV does not run them.
For the meaning of these states and joint versus per-scan statistics, see


bounds, sharing and fit statistics.

parameter_kind distinguishes varying, fixed, linked and static.
Lorentzian/Voigt gamma is included as a static specification, not as an
optimised width. Unused EMG gamma is excluded. A missing standard error is blank,
not zero. Infinite bounds are written as -inf and inf.

Peak A is intrinsic integrated area, not height. Exported peak curves also
include gain and optional component scaling. EMG mu is not necessarily the
position of its maximum. Preserve these distinctions when analysing the CSV.

The table includes the saved fitting range, evaluation count and fit statistics.
For simultaneous fits, statistics_scope is simultaneous series: chisqr,
redchi and ndata describe the joint optimisation. spectrum_chisqr and
spectrum_ndata describe the individual scan. Strict trend fits have no covariance
estimate, so their standard errors remain blank.

is fitted; overlay curves remain comparisons. The worker uses a snapshot while
editing is disabled. A progress window shows residual evaluations and elapsed time.
Its bar represents the fraction of the evaluation budget, not a prediction of

stop. The worker checks at evaluation boundaries; an evaluation already running
must return first. The window stays open with a stopping message until the worker

model and previous successful result. Wait for completion before closing the main
window.

Fitting requires finite, strictly increasing measured energy. A native scan can
contain small backward steps, including early monochromator jitter or backlash.
The GUI detects the ordering problem; it does not diagnose the instrument cause
or silently reorder it.

Review measured-energy order reports the filename, point count, backward steps,
repeated energy points and the first non-increasing step. Its graph plots measured
energy against acquired point number, initially near the first problem. This
is an acquisition-order diagnostic, rather than the fitted intensity spectrum.

available when inspecting the sorted preview.

point numbers identify where each measurement came from.

or Skip scan to leave it unimported.

The reviewed choice sorts display/fitting arrays by measured energy for every
channel, maintaining paired detector values. It preserves all measurements and
does not average, interpolate, smooth or trim points. Native processing still uses

order, the native dictionary and source bytes remain retained in complete sessions.

panel; cancel that panel if you do not want to proceed.

Exact duplicate energies cannot form a strictly increasing axis. Nonfinite selected
energy/intensity values and too few points also need explicit resolution. The GUI
does not average duplicates or drop bad rows to make a file fit.

columns with non-increasing energy are rejected with an import error; they do not

records.content:
Suppose P2 should lie 1.8–2.2 eV above P1, while P1 can move within its own bounds.

Add both peaks and give them distinct names.

Open Peak constraints… above the parameter table.

Set Target peak to P2, Reference peak to P1 and Parameter to μ position.

Choose Within a range. Enter initial separation 2.0, minimum 1.8
and maximum 2.2 eV.

Click Add / update constraint, check the list, then Apply.

The model now uses P2_mu = P1_mu + delta_P2_mu. The separation is an independent
fitted parameter inside [1.8, 2.2]; P2’s position is derived. Put the absolute
allowed energy range on P1 and edit the generated separation to change the link.
This keeps the interval relative to P1 as P1 moves.

The target’s old independent value/bounds/Free settings are preserved but inactive
while linked. They do not additionally clip the calculated target. Check the
reference and separation bounds together when deciding physically allowed positions.
EMG μ means the underlying Gaussian position, so the displayed peak maxima need
not have that same separation.

Choose Exact offset / equality to keep a fixed separation. An exact position
offset of 2.0 gives P2 μ = P1 μ + 2.0. An exact sigma offset of zero gives equal
Gaussian sigma values. These are additive relations, not ratios.

The Parameter dropdown offers only parameters active on both selected shapes:
μ and A where supported, sigma for Gaussian/Voigt/EMG, and tau for EMG pairs.
Static gamma is not a fitted/linkable coordinate. Equal areas do not imply equal
heights when widths/shapes differ; equal Voigt sigma does not also tie gamma.

Select an existing constraint to edit it, or Remove selected constraint to
make its target independent again. Apply commits the dialog as one Undo step;
Cancel discards its staged edits. Cycles, self-links and incompatible references
are rejected. Rename updates supported relationships; removal of a peak needed
by a link requires resolving the dependency first.



Figure 1:A staged relative-position constraint on synthetic model components.

To keep an edge a specified energy distance from a component:

Add the required edges using Add ionisation edge, if absent, and add their controlling peaks.

Optionally select an edge or controlling peak in the component list or plot.

Click Link/Unlink edge to μ… in Component controls.

When multiple edges are present, choose Edge. With one edge, this selector
is hidden. Check Link edge to peak μ, choose the controlling Peak, enter
the exact Offset (eV). Cancel discards panel changes.

Switch edges to configure other links if needed, then Apply once. Check each
edge’s position relationship in the parameter table. Moving or fitting a
controlling peak moves its linked edges with it.



Figure 2:One edge keeps the panel compact, without an Edge selector.



Figure 3:Multiple edges add one selector. Changes across edges are staged together until Apply;
switching the selector alone does not add links. Cancel discards all staged edits.

The relation is E_edge = selected peak μ + offset. For peak μ = 285.00 eV,
an offset of +0.20 gives E_edge = 285.20 eV; a negative offset places it below μ.
It is an exact offset, not an independent fitted separation. For EMG the source
is its underlying μ, not its observed maximum. The model dE shifts both displayed
positions consistently, without changing their native separation.

Linking replaces the edge’s independent position bounds/Free setting with the
derived position; put absolute position bounds on the controlling peak’s μ.
In simultaneous fits, the edge’s global/per-spectrum scope follows that peak μ.
To change the peak or offset, reopen the same panel. An existing link’s peak and
offset appear initially, even if another component is selected. To release the
relationship, select the edge, clear Link edge to peak μ and Apply. This keeps the current derived edge
energy, makes E_edge free and resets its bounds to unbounded; review Min/Max/Free
before fitting it independently. The link/unlink model edit can be undone.

Each edge can follow a different peak, or several edges can follow the same peak
with different signed offsets. Width, step and post-slope stay independently
configured. All edges’ linked positions use the same native exact-offset convention
and inherit the controlling peak’s effective global/per-spectrum scope in series fits.
Renaming a controlling peak updates its edge links; unlink before removing a peak
that still controls an edge. Linked models retain these relationships when saved,
reopened or exported. Linking a peak does not insert a missing physical feature into the data.
If the button is unavailable, check that at least one peak and edge exist.
Select the controlling peak inside the panel; no plot selection is required.
Add an edge rather than expecting the link command to create one. For
links between peaks with a fitted separation interval, use the peak-constraint
procedure above instead.

In a simultaneous series fit, an independent parameter can be global or
per_spectrum. A linked target inherits the scope required by its source/separation;
its Sharing may therefore be inferred and unavailable for direct editing. Restrict
the controlling reference or delta_<target> when adding series bounds/trends.

After optional I0/PD correction, intensity preparation subtracts the mean in the
baseline window. Scale method then selects the denominator:

Mean to one (default): mean of the baseline-subtracted signal in the scale window.

Area to one (trapezoidal): signed integral of that signal against measured
energy, using consecutive points inside the scale window. It requires at least
two points and a nonzero finite area. Endpoints are not interpolated or extrapolated.

Area scaling accounts for unequal energy spacing; it makes the measured window’s
integral one, rather than its average height. It also changes the prepared signal’s
units relative to mean scaling. Negative signed areas are allowed, as negative
means are in mean mode. Choose suitable windows and inspect the preview. These
preparation areas are distinct from individual fitted peak areas A.

The native engine supplies baseline/mean preparation; optional area scaling is
implemented in the GUI’s Qt-independent preparation wrapper. Existing sessions
without a scale-method setting keep mean scaling. The choice and denominator
are retained with the processed channels and session. See also


scientific conventions.

The PD acquisition is I0-normalised and, when selected, independently energy
aligned. Its response is interpolated for division over the common energy
range. The overlap can shorten the prepared spectrum; inspect the preview and
retained point counts. Missing references, zero denominators and unsuitable
windows are errors to resolve, not reasons to silently invent a correction.

Preparation and fitting are separate collection operations. This chapter covers
the implemented fitting controls and staged review. Practise with the


synthetic series exercise, or follow the


acquisition workflow with your own data.

Start by fitting a representative spectrum and inspecting its residuals,
components, bounds and constraints. This reference model is the starting point
for the collection workflow. The current working model is used, including edits
since its last successful fit. It does not establish that every later spectrum
has the same physical interpretation.

Sharing dropdowns in the main parameter table matter for simultaneous fitting.
global means one value across targets; per_spectrum gives each target an
independent value. A label such as “bulk” does not create sharing automatically.

For example, share peak μ and sigma globally while letting A vary per spectrum

model assumption, not a claim that every series should have constant widths.

In GUI 0.2.25, the Spectrum / residual tab shows the selected staged target
and its data-minus-model residual. Its label identifies the scan and reviewed pass.
Failed or unstaged rows clear the previous curves and show their status, so a
neighbouring successful fit cannot be mistaken for that target. The preview covers
the loaded grid; optimisation still uses each target’s chosen fitting domain.

Open Parameter trends / compare passes, then choose a parameter. Blue is pass
one and orange is pass two; both remain visible when available. Red crosses mark
reported bound hits. Missing/failed targets leave gaps rather than zero values.
The adjacent table reports values, available standard errors, bounds flags and
per-pass status. Fixed parameters are labelled and have no error bars; copied
models are identified as copies. Available bars are ±1 local standard error, not
total experimental uncertainties; 

statistics limitations
still apply, including unavailable covariance for strict fits.

The review-axis dropdown offers selected scan order, the configured numeric
coordinate, and incidence angle when recognised degree-valued scan metadata is
available. Angle values follow the scan-table source/convention, including the
identified R1 correction; missing angles remain gaps. These display choices do
not reorder targets, change trend constraints or invalidate a fit. Native model
parameter values match the parameter table: EMG μ is not its maximum, and μ is
not shifted into displayed-energy coordinates. Shared parameters can legitimately
form a constant series. Click a plotted point or review-table row to select that
scan in the target table; use the spectrum tab to inspect its curve.



Figure 1:Synthetic comparison: independent widths in pass one, fixed mean width in pass
two. This illustrates the effect of an imposed assumption, not evidence that the
second pass is physically preferable.

Use 

two-pass review
to choose which pass Apply commits. Changing the plotted parameter or review
axis does not change that choice.

Series constraints… can narrow selected parameters relative to the original
reference using absolute or percentage windows, or fix them to reference values.
These limits intersect the source model’s bounds. They do not drift with each
previous-fit seed. Use a physically motivated tolerance rather than making all
parameters nearly immovable.

Linked targets remain derived. Restrict their reference or separation parameter
instead of imposing an independent bound that the target cannot honour.
This includes every linked ionisation-edge position: each follows its controlling
peak’s effective scope. Configure those links in the


edge panel before staging.

Series-constraint choice

Example / meaning

Keep reference bounds

Keep the existing allowed interval

Absolute tolerance

μ = 285.20, Below/Above = 0.05 eV gives 285.15–285.25 eV before intersection

Percentage tolerance

sigma = 0.30, Below/Above = 5% gives 0.285–0.315 eV before intersection

Fix to reference

Hold the reference value; Free becomes false without setting equal bounds

Bounds are intersected with the reference’s existing interval, so a tolerance
cannot widen it. Percentages use abs(reference value); a zero reference requires
an absolute tolerance or Fix. Below/Above can differ, must be nonnegative and
cannot both be zero for a tolerance rule. Fixed, linked and static rows explain
their roles instead of being silently freed. Review Effective series bounds
before staging; Ctrl/Shift and the selected-row controls can apply a rule to many rows.

These limits stay centred on the original reference, even in previous-success
seeding mode. Seeding changes the start, not the allowed reference interval. They
are hard bounds, not automatically inferred uncertainties. Accepted recipes are
saved with the source-channel session view; applied targets retain ordinary
bounds/fixed states and provenance. Saving only the source model does not activate
its separate collection recipe.

Trends / pass-two setup… supports soft penalties or strict constraints for
monotonic evolution, a straight-line trend, smoothness, endpoints, maximum
step/slope or curvature, and an identified scan as a maximum/minimum. A chosen
extremum can also have monotonic sides. These rules couple scans and require a
simultaneous fit.

Choose equal scan order or explicitly enter increasing numeric coordinates such
as time or dose. Coordinates define spacing for derivative limits; their units
therefore affect the meaning of a maximum slope/curvature. Scan order is an
explicit input, not an inferred acquisition chronology.

A soft penalty encourages a trend. It does not guarantee it. Strict constraints
use a separate constrained solver; see 

constraints and statistics
for the distinction and its uncertainty limitations.

Open Trends / pass-two setup… → Overall trends, add a rule and select an active
independent per_spectrum parameter. A global parameter already has one value
across the series. For a linked target, select its controlling source/separation.
Choose whether the rules apply to pass one, pass two or both.

Rule

Soft strength

Strict strength

Increasing / decreasing

Penalise adjacent violations beyond fractional tolerance

Non-decreasing / non-increasing

Maximum / minimum at selected scan

Encourage the named acquisition to dominate the others

Named acquisition at least / at most every other target

Smooth curvature

Penalise curvature, optionally in log space

Exact straight line

Small steps

Penalise adjacent changes, optionally in log space

Constant value

Final / initial ratio

Encourage the chosen ratio

Exact ratio

Final value

Encourage the chosen endpoint

Exact endpoint

Maximum absolute slope

Penalise excess above the chosen maximum

Bound absolute slope

Maximum absolute curvature

Penalise excess above the chosen maximum

Bound absolute curvature

In particular, strict “small steps” means zero step. Use maximum absolute
slope for a nonzero allowed step limit. Equal scan order gives slope units per
scan; numeric time/dose gives units per time/dose. A maximum curvature is a
second-derivative restriction, not an energy-width bound.

Soft Weight is lambda: penalty residuals scale by its square root. Floor
protects relative/log calculations. Fraction tolerance is a fraction (0.02
means 2%), not an entered percentage; it is distinct from the percentage-tolerance
columns in Series constraints. Target is the endpoint, ratio or nonnegative maximum
for rules that use it. Inactive cells are retained but ignored.

records.content:
Choose the named scan in Extremum scan; it must also be checked as a target.
Extremum only compares it with all other selected targets. Monotonic sides
additionally imposes rise/fall for a maximum or fall/rise for a minimum in the chosen
order. Ties/plateaus are allowed, and an endpoint can be the extremum. The anchor
follows the acquisition when rows move; it is not silently changed to the largest
fitted value or implicitly checked as a target.

For a middle scan expected to have the largest P2 area, choose P2_A, Maximum at
selected scan, that middle acquisition and the appropriate strength. Choose
Monotonic sides only if intermediate scans should also follow that shape. This
does not constrain any later coverage or kinetic calculation.

Use Move scan up/down to set the order explicitly. Numeric coordinates must
increase strictly for selected targets; equal/reversed values are rejected instead
of sorted. Coordinate units are chosen by the user. A limit of 0.1 area per minute
is different from 0.1 area per second. Soft nonuniform smoothness normalises mean
spacing; maximum derivative limits always use the actual coordinate units.

Infeasible strict rules/bounds or a nonconverged joint fit produce no successful
joint stage. Strict constraints are not huge penalties and currently have no
covariance/stderr estimate; only budget/ftol apply. Soft-only fits use least squares
with all three tolerances. Joint statistics can include penalty residuals; inspect
data agreement separately. See 

fitting and results.

Stage the selected targets, inspect successes, failures and fitted curves, then
choose Apply successful results. Failed/unselected scans retain their work.
Cancelling discards staged changes; cancelling a running job requests a safe
stop and waits for its worker.

For averaging, sharing promotion and tighter second-pass windows, follow


two-pass fitting. Merely running either pass does not
replace working scans. Choose the reviewed successful fits in the


CSV export selector after applying them.

collection; a model is a reusable fitting template. Numerical CSV reports are

To resume it, choose Session → Open session and select that session JSON.
Opening a session restores its saved workspace rather than adding a scan to
the existing collection; respond to any current-work save/discard prompt deliberately.

Complete sessions retain the loaded spectra, native acquisition dictionaries and
source bytes, separate PD references, prepared/intermediate channels, processing
settings, active selection, per-channel models and successful fit results. They
also retain fit settings and saved browser/display choices. Native acquisitions
are embedded so reopening is not dependent on their original file paths remaining
available. Plain text/CSV imports retain their selected arrays/basic import settings,
not a complete native acquisition they never contained.

Complete sessions also retain each acquisition’s 

editable notes,
independently of its selected detector and original comment. Older sessions without
notes reopen with empty notes. Save the session after editing; a model-only file
or fit CSV report does not preserve these annotations.

Model Undo/Redo histories and temporary Messages history are not persisted across
restarts. Saving records the current working model and retained successful results;
later model edits can mean those two models differ. 

Last fit results and CSV export
refer to the retained successful snapshot, not an unrun trial.

GUI 0.2.27 sessions also retain 

workspace arrangements:
panel visibility, docking/tabs, floating geometry and section expansion. These
are separate from per-channel model/display values. Large-screen standard layouts
adapt on smaller windows, and off-screen floating geometry is constrained.

The standalone application writes a separate recovery checkpoint approximately
every 60 seconds while committed work is unsaved and the workspace is idle.
It also requests one before a single fit, preparation or series workflow. It skips
active drags, modal dialogs and running fits/workflows. Session → Save recovery
checkpoint now requests a copy immediately when eligible. Snapshot capture may
briefly pause very large collections; disk writing runs in a background worker.

Recovery copies use the same complete session representation, including raw
acquisitions, channel models/results, preparation, notes and view settings. They
exclude unapplied modal drafts, model Undo history and temporary messages. They
are written atomically to the application’s local-data recovery folder
(normally %LOCALAPPDATA%\NEXAFSFit GUI\recovery on Windows), separately from
your saved session and source files. They do not mark the workspace saved.

After an interruption, startup offers Restore selected, Keep for later
or Discard selected. Session → Recover interrupted work… reopens this
choice later. Restore validates the checkpoint and opens it as unsaved work;
review it and save an ordinary session. It does not overwrite its former session.
Keep leaves the file available. Discard deletes only the chosen recovery copy.
Checkpoints belonging to another running instance are excluded using process locks.
An unreadable or unsupported checkpoint is retained unless explicitly discarded.

Each running window owns its own recovery file. A successful manual session save
or session opening clears that window’s old copy. A normal close after the usual
Save/Discard decision also clears its copy; unchosen checkpoints from earlier runs
remain available. If a checkpoint is being written, let it finish and close again.
Failed writes keep the preceding complete copy and report a warning; save manually.
Changes since the last completed checkpoint can still be lost during an interruption.
Periodic recovery is enabled by the standalone launcher, not automatically by an
embedded Workspace.

Choose Model → Save model to write the current components, parameter values,
bounds, Free/Sharing states and supported links as versioned JSON. It does not
save the loaded acquisition collection or its preparation/metadata. Use a session
when you need to reproduce the complete working dataset and its processing.

For reuse, import/select the new data first, then Model → Open model. The
model is applied to that active channel while its data, preparation and fit range
remain in place. A supported session file can also supply just its active model.
Other scans keep their own work. See 

the model-reuse procedure.

Model import clears the active fit statistics because they do not describe a fit
of the imported model to these data. Undo can restore the previous model; run a
new fit before treating the imported model as a successful result.

The History menu’s Undo/Redo acts on the active scan/channel’s model edits,
including completed drags, constraints, imported models and successful fitted
values. It is distinct from the Messages panel’s History… record of feedback.
Switching channels restores their independent model work rather than sharing one
global Undo stack across all datasets.

Preparation and collection operations are not one collection-wide model Undo.
Save a checkpoint before replacing prepared signals or applying a large series
workflow. Preparation invalidates fits against the affected replacement data;
unavailable cached channels may be labelled previous preparation. Review the


channel/stage guide when returning to older work.

Accepted series recipes and applied result provenance can be stored in sessions,
including selected pass-two seeds/windows and first-pass provenance. Merely
staging a fit in an open dialog is not a persistent checkpoint. Apply/review the
intended pass before saving; see

The application validates saved files before replacement. An unsupported version
or invalid model/session reports an error while retaining current working state.
Compatibility notices can identify preserved but inactive fields, such as unused
EMG gamma. Those fields are not evidence that a new physical parameter is active.

Do not remove fields or edit recorded results merely to suppress a warning. Keep
the original file, record the exact error and application version, and distinguish
Open model from Open session when reporting what you were trying to restore.
Preserved source records and supported migrations are handled by the session loader;
this page is not an instruction to execute content from JSON files.

A soft trend adds penalty residuals to the data residual vector. Its strength and
tolerance control a preference: a finite penalty does not mathematically guarantee
monotonicity, a chosen endpoint or a maximum step.

Strict trends impose inequalities/equalities through a constrained optimiser.
In this GUI they use an adapter-side SLSQP path; ordinary unconstrained-by-trends
fits use the existing least-squares/TRF path. Strict trends are not a new native
lineshape or a modification of the measured spectra.

Trend rules couple selected spectra. Scan order or explicit coordinates define
their spacing. Nonuniform time/dose coordinates change derivative limits and must
be interpreted in the chosen units. An identified maximum/minimum refers to a
particular scan, not simply to whichever scan currently has the largest fitted value.

For ordered per-scan values p_i and strictly increasing coordinates x_i, the
maximum-slope rule uses s_i=(p_{i+1}-p_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i). The maximum-curvature
rule uses c_i=2(s_{i+1}-s_i)/(x_{i+2}-x_i). Strict rules bound their absolute
values; soft versions penalise excess over the chosen nonnegative maximum.
With equal-order spacing, the units are parameter/scan and parameter/scan².
Changing time/dose units changes numerical derivative limits.

Strict increasing/decreasing and extrema allow ties. A straight-line constraint
means zero curvature; constant-value means zero adjacent change. Neither means
“small but nonzero”: use explicit derivative maxima for that. Soft log smoothing
does not imply log-space strict inequalities; strict trends use linear values.

The data residual is measured intensity minus model. Unweighted chi-square
is the sum of squared residuals over the selected fit domain. Its numerical scale
depends on the intensity units/preparation. A smaller chi-square alone does not
prove that a more complex model is scientifically preferable.

Last fit results reports evaluations, chi-square, reduced chi-square and
information criteria. Check systematic residual structure, values at bounds,
sensitivity to the fit domain and whether parameters are identifiable. The current
single-spectrum GUI does not provide a general uncertainty-weight editor.

A reported standard error is a local covariance-based estimate when available.
It is not a complete assessment of calibration error, preprocessing choices,
model inadequacy or correlated parameters. An unavailable error is blank in CSV,
not zero. A bound-hit indicator is a prompt to inspect the chosen limits.

For simultaneous fits, joint statistics describe the entire optimisation;
per-scan chi-square and point counts are reported separately. Soft penalty terms
can contribute to the joint objective. Do not interpret that total as only a
single scan’s spectral misfit.

Strict-trend fits currently have no covariance/stderr estimate. Their reduced
chi-square and information criteria are approximate because active inequalities
are not subtracted from the degrees of freedom. Only ftol and the evaluation
budget apply to this path; xtol/gtol are inactive.

This reference summarises the supplied NEXAFSFit evaluator used by GUI 0.2.24
throughout this manual. The equations describe the implemented generic
model, rather than a choice of alternative textbook edge models.

The model evaluates profiles at effective energyE_{\mathrm{eff}} = E + dE.

A symmetric peak with native position mu is therefore plotted at mu - dE.
Energy alignment during preparation changes the data energy axis; dE is a
separate optional model parameter. Do not confuse the two.
The 

reference-calibration definition describes
the acquisition offset; 

GUI preparation shows how to apply it.

Each peak contribution isI_p(E) = g\,s_p\,A_p\,f_p(E_{\mathrm{eff}}),

where gain is the global factor g, scale_param optionally names a scale s,
and the profile f has unit area over the full energy axis. Omitted gain and scale
act as one. A is intrinsic integrated area; the plotted contribution has area
g s A over the infinite domain. A finite scan/window generally captures less.
The 

position/area drag controls
convert a requested component height back into this integrated-area convention.

A group name only collects peak sums. Assigning a peak to “bulk” does not multiply
its area, share its width or constrain its position.

Shape ID

Adjustable shape parameters

Width convention

mu; gamma is static

Every shape also has integrated area A. Active parameters can be fixed or varied;
“adjustable” does not mean every value should be allowed to move in every fit.



Figure 1:Profiles generated by the actual engine at mu = 0, sigma = 0.3 eV,
gamma = 0.2 eV and EMG tau = 0.5 eV. The plotted interval is finite.

For a Gaussian,f_G(x)=\frac{\exp[-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)]}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}.

Its FWHM is approximately 2.355 sigma, and its height at unit gain/scale is
A / (sigma * sqrt(2*pi)).

For a Lorentzian,f_L(x)=\frac{\gamma}{\pi[(x-\mu)^2+\gamma^2]}.

Its FWHM is 2 gamma. The engine evaluates the unit-area Voigt with the Faddeeva
function. Voigt sigma and gamma describe the Gaussian and Lorentzian constituents;
neither is the total Voigt FWHM.

The engine uses its stable Delley EMG implementation. mu is the underlying
Gaussian mean. Positive tau produces the higher-energy tail used by this GUI,
and the apparent maximum generally differs from mu. Tau approaching zero gives
the Gaussian limit. The editor restricts tau to nonnegative values; it does not
offer a separate negative-tau tail interpretation.

Top-level gamma is a static specification for Lorentzian/Voigt. It is unused by
EMG, even when retained in an older model. Do not interpret an unused gamma as an
extra EMG broadening.
For the corresponding numerical and graphical controls, see


model parameter states
and 

EMG asymmetry dragging.

The linear background lies outside global gain:B(E)=b_0+b_1\left(E_{\mathrm{eff}}-\overline{E_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right).

The mean is taken over the full grid supplied to evaluation. The GUI evaluates
on the complete spectrum before applying a fit mask, keeping that reference
stable when the fitting range is narrowed. Cropping arrays before calling a
native evaluator instead changes this reference.

The generic edge uses the smooth stepS(E)=\frac12\left[1+\operatorname{erf}
\left(\frac{E_{\mathrm{eff}}-E_{\mathrm{edge}}}{\sqrt{2}\,w_{\mathrm{edge}}}\right)\right],

with contributionI_{\mathrm{edge}}(E)=g\,[h+m(E_{\mathrm{eff}}-E_{\mathrm{edge}})]\,S(E).

Here h is edge_step, m is post_slope and w is w_edge. Multiple GUI edges
add contributions with this same convention. The total is background plus edges
plus peaks. Background, gain and model shift are optional in new GUI models.

Avoid adding redundant gain/scale/area freedoms unless you have a way to identify
them: several multiplicative parameters can trade off without establishing a
unique physical area.
Use the 

model editor
to add those terms, 

edge-to-peak links
to relate positions, or 

edge subtraction
to inspect their visual contribution without changing the fitting arrays.

Native calibrate_energy_with_reference_foil locates a chosen maximum/minimum
of reference/I0 within a search window on the original measured energy axis.
argextreme selects the measured extreme. parab3 refines it with the vertex of
the quadratic through that sample and its two immediate in-window neighbours
in acquisition order. At a window boundary it falls back to the measured point;
degenerate or linear three-point inputs also use the centre point. This is local
interpolation, not an independently optimised peak-shape fit.

The data offset is target_energy - feature_energy, applied equally to all
parallel acquisition channels. A separate photodiode acquisition is calibrated
independently. No baseline/scale windows are involved in finding this reference
feature. The later baseline and scale windows use aligned energies. This data
alignment offset is distinct from the model’s optional dE.

Choose reference windows and targets appropriate to the acquisition. The native
function can construct reference/I0 when absent; its method default is argextreme,
whereas the GUI initially selects parab3. The GUI’s optional inspection panel
retains the native input trace and output feature/offset. Its local curve uses
the same three-point formula without rerunning calibration or modifying the result.
An out-of-window native vertex is reported without silently moving or clipping it.

For a baseline window W_b, preparation first subtracts
b=\operatorname{mean}_{E_i\in W_b} y_i. Mean scaling uses
D=\operatorname{mean}_{E_i\in W_s}(y_i-b) and returns (y_i-b)/D.
This is the unchanged native prepare_fitting_signal behaviour and the GUI default.
The native function has no selectable area-method argument.

The GUI’s optional area scaling instead uses
D=\sum_i (E_{i+1}-E_i)[(y_i-b)+(y_{i+1}-b)]/2, over consecutive
measured points inside W_s. At least two distinct points and a finite nonzero
denominator are required. The integration is signed, accounts for unequal energy
spacing and adds no interpolated endpoints. It uses increasing measured energy;
an acquisition with reversals first requires the user’s explicit sorting review.

This area denominator has signal-times-energy units. Setting the prepared window
integral to one differs from setting its average height to one; neither quantity
is an individual model peak area A. Baseline subtraction still uses a mean in
both modes. Settings, native intermediates and actual scale denominators are
retained without changing original data. See the 

GUI preparation procedure.
